subsection: 4. The Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989

notes.h: What judicial separation is (Higher Level only)
notes.b: When a marriage breaks down and the couple cannot agree how to part, a court can step in. Judicial separation under the Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989, as amended, is a court decree under which spouses live apart with the court's orders in place. It does not end the marriage.
points: A decree (a formal order of the court) means the spouses are no longer required to live together, and the court sets out the arrangements for their maintenance and property.
Because the marriage continues, neither spouse is free to remarry after a judicial separation. Only a divorce ends a marriage and allows remarriage.
The application is made to the Circuit Court or the High Court, either of which can grant a judicial separation, and it is heard by a judge. It is not made to the District Court.
A judicial separation is a legal status that the court grants, unlike informal separation, which spouses agree between themselves without a court order.
It is needed in particular where the couple cannot agree the terms of separating. If they can agree, they use a separation agreement instead.
notes.tip: If asked why a person cannot remarry after a judicial separation, answer that the marriage still exists. When asked which court, name the Circuit Court or the High Court.

notes.h: Grounds for judicial separation (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A court will not grant a decree just because a spouse asks for one. The applicant (the spouse applying) must prove at least one ground, or reason, set out in the Act. The Act has six grounds, and the respondent is the other spouse.
points: Adultery by the respondent spouse since the marriage.
Unreasonable behaviour by the respondent that makes it unreasonable for the applicant to continue living with them.
Desertion by the respondent for a continuous period of at least one year immediately before the application.
The spouses have lived apart for at least one year and both consent to the decree being granted.
The spouses have lived apart for at least three years, even if the other spouse does not consent.

The marriage has broken down so that a normal marital relationship has not existed between the spouses for at least one year before the application. This is the ground most commonly used because it does not require either spouse to be at fault.
The applicant must establish one of these statutory grounds (grounds set by law) before the court can grant the decree.
notes.tip: Do not give only adultery, unreasonable behaviour and desertion as the full list. The Act has six grounds, and leaving out the living-apart and no normal marital relationship grounds loses marks. Name at least four, and all six if you can.

notes.h: Orders the court can make (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A decree on its own only releases the spouses from living together. The court can add orders that settle money, property and children, so the practical questions are answered at the same time.
points: Maintenance orders require one spouse to provide financial support (regular payments for living costs) for the other spouse and for the children.
Property orders divide or transfer property between the spouses, including who lives in the family home (property adjustment), and orders can also be made about the use of the family home.
Orders on the custody of children decide where a child lives and who has responsibility for their upbringing.
Access orders set out the arrangements for a parent who does not have custody to see the child.
The court may extinguish succession rights, which means a spouse loses their right to inherit from the other spouse. Without such an order, the right to inherit continues.
A pension adjustment order is also possible.
These orders can be made together with the decree, so that the financial and childcare arrangements are settled at once, which saves the family returning to court.
Maintenance orders made on judicial separation can later be varied by the court if the circumstances of either spouse change, such as a change in income.
notes.tip: Examiners ask what the Act provides, so cover maintenance, property, children (custody and access) and extinguishing succession rights. Inheritance rights end only if the court so orders, not automatically.

notes.b: Judicial separation sits between informal arrangements and divorce. Comparing it with a separation agreement and with divorce shows who decides in each case and whether the marriage ends.
points: Judicial separation differs from divorce because divorce ends the marriage and allows both spouses to remarry, while judicial separation does not.
Divorce requires the spouses to have lived apart for at least two of the previous three years (Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 as amended by the Family Law Act 2019), and it ends the marriage.
A separation agreement (a deed of separation, sometimes called a legal separation) is a binding agreement made between the spouses, whereas judicial separation is a decree made by the court.
A separation agreement is drawn up by solicitors and agreed by both spouses, often with a mediator. It is cheaper and avoids court, and it is legally binding.
Judicial separation is used when the spouses cannot agree terms, because the judge decides for them.
In both a separation agreement and judicial separation, the spouses are not required to live together, but they remain married.
notes.tip: In a legal options question, compare the separation agreement (the spouses decide), judicial separation (the court decides) and divorce (ends the marriage). For each, say who decides, whether the marriage ends and whether remarriage is allowed. For a full answer give the grounds, the court, the orders, and that remarriage is not allowed.

keyTerms.definition: A court decree under which spouses live apart without the marriage being dissolved, with the court setting out maintenance and property arrangements.
A formal order of the court that grants a judicial separation or divorce.
The spouse against whom an application for judicial separation is made.
One spouse leaving the other without reasonable cause and without the other's consent, for a continuous period.
A court order setting out when a parent who does not have custody may see a child.
A court order deciding with whom a child lives and who is responsible for the child's upbringing.
A court order that divides or transfers property between spouses when the marriage is ending.

factCards.term: Grounds for judicial separation under the 1989 Act
factCards.definition: Adultery, unreasonable behaviour, and desertion for at least one year.

factCards.term: Courts that can grant judicial separation
factCards.definition: The Circuit Court or the High Court.

factCards.term: Status of spouses after judicial separation
factCards.definition: The marriage continues, so neither spouse can remarry.

factCards.term: Orders that can accompany a judicial separation
factCards.definition: Maintenance, property, custody and access orders.

questions.prompt: Explain why a spouse cannot remarry after a judicial separation.
questions.model: A judicial separation is a court decree that allows spouses to live apart, but it does not end the marriage. Because the marriage continues to exist in law, neither spouse is free to remarry. Only divorce ends the marriage and permits remarriage.

questions.prompt: Outline the grounds on which a spouse may seek judicial separation under the Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989, and the orders a court may make.
questions.model: The grounds include adultery by the respondent spouse since the marriage, unreasonable behaviour by the respondent that makes it unreasonable for the applicant to continue living with them, and desertion for a continuous period of at least one year immediately before the application. The application is made to the Circuit Court or the High Court. If the decree is granted, the marriage continues, so neither spouse may remarry. The court can make maintenance orders for the spouse and the children, property orders that divide or transfer property including the family home, custody orders deciding where a child lives, and access orders setting out contact arrangements for a parent without custody. These orders can be made together with the decree so that the arrangements are settled at the same time.
